When the function returns, the return address is popped off the stack and used to jump back to the calling function. If a buffer overflow occurs and data is written to the stack, it can overwrite the return address. When the function returns, the corrupted return address may point to an incorrect location, causing the program to jump to an unintended location, potentially executing malicious code.

The dead man's switch is typically a lever, button, or pedal that the operator must keep pressed down at all times while operating the machinery. If the operator lets go of the switch for any reason, such as falling unconscious or being knocked unconscious, the machinery will automatically shut down to prevent any potential harm to the operator or others nearby.

In some cases, the dead man's switch may be integrated into the control panel of the machinery, requiring the operator to continuously monitor and confirm that the switch is still engaged. This helps ensure that the machinery remains safe and operational until the operator resumes control or a backup system takes over.
